stem:
\[ x^2-5x-24=0 \]
What is the sum of the solutions to the given equation?
whyCorrect: You do not have to find the solutions. For \(ax^2+bx+c=0\), the sum of the solutions is \(-\frac{b}{a}=-\frac{-5}{1}=5\). Factoring confirms it: \((x-8)(x+3)=0\) gives 8 and \(-3\), which sum to 5.

stem: The function \(f\) gives the product of a number, \(x\), and a number that is 91 more than \(x\). Which equation defines \(f\) ?
whyCorrect: “91 more than \(x\)” is \(x+91\), and “the product” means multiply the two: \(f(x)=x(x+91)=x^2+91x\). Distribute rather than just writing the two pieces side by side.

whyWrong.A: The leading sign is wrong and this adds the two quantities in part instead of multiplying them.
whyWrong.B: This is \(x^2+91\), which is what you get by adding 91 to \(x^2\); the \(x\) that multiplies the 91 is missing.
whyWrong.D: The extra \(+91\) is left over from expanding as though there were a third term. \(x(x+91)\) has only two terms.

stem:
\[ x^2-100=0 \]
How many distinct real solutions does this given equation have?
whyCorrect: Add 100 to both sides: \(x^2=100\), so \(x=10\) or \(x=-10\). A square root equation like this has two solutions, one positive and one negative, because both \(10^2\) and \((-10)^2\) equal 100.

whyWrong.A: There would be no real solution only if \(x^2\) had to equal a negative number, e.g. \(x^2+100=0\).
whyWrong.B: Taking only the principal root \(x=10\) misses \(x=-10\). One solution happens when the equation is a perfect square set to zero, like \((x-10)^2=0\).
whyWrong.D: Infinitely many solutions requires an identity true for every \(x\); here only two values work.

stem:
\[ \frac{x}{(x-1)(x+1)}=\frac{81}{56x} \]
Which of the following is a solution to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Recognise \((x-1)(x+1)=x^2-1\) and cross multiply: \(56x\cdot x=81(x^2-1)\), so \(56x^2=81x^2-81\). That gives \(25x^2=81\), \(x^2=\frac{81}{25}\), and \(x=\pm\frac{9}{5}\). Only \(\frac{9}{5}\) appears among the choices.

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{1}{5}\) keeps the denominator 5 but loses the \(\sqrt{81}=9\) in the numerator.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{9}{25}\) takes the square root of the numerator only. Both numerator and denominator have to be rooted: \(\sqrt{\frac{81}{25}}=\frac{9}{5}\).
whyWrong.C: \(x=1\) makes the factor \(x-1\) zero, so the left side is undefined. It can never be a solution no matter what the algebra suggests.

stem:
\[ 3w^2+11w-c=0 \]
In the given equation, \(c\) is a constant. A solution to the given equation is \(\frac{-11+\sqrt{433}}{6}\). What is the value of \(c\) ?
whyCorrect: Write what the quadratic formula would give: with \(a=3\), \(b=11\) and constant term \(-c\), \(w=\frac{-11\pm\sqrt{121+12c}}{6}\). Match that against the given solution: the denominators and the \(-11\) already agree, so \(121+12c=433\), giving \(12c=312\) and \(c=26\).

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=3\left(\frac{1}{4}-x\right)^2+\frac{13}{4}\). What is the value of \(f\!\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\) ?
whyCorrect: Substituting \(x=\frac{1}{4}\) makes the bracket \(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{4}=0\), so the squared term contributes nothing and \(f\!\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)=\frac{13}{4}\). Look for the input that zeroes the bracket before doing any arithmetic.

stem:
\[ f(x)=-16x^2+99 \]
The function \(f\) gives the estimated height, in feet, of an acorn \(x\) seconds after the acorn fell from a tree. Based on the function, what is the estimated height, in feet, of an acorn before it fell from the tree?
whyCorrect: “Before it fell” is the moment the fall begins, \(x=0\). Substituting gives \(f(0)=99\). The constant term of a falling-object model is always the starting height.

stem: The variables \(x\) and \(y\) have a quadratic relationship. When x = 0, y = 45. When x = 6, y = 81. When x = 15, y = 0. Which equation represents this relationship?
whyCorrect: Test the three given points rather than deriving the equation. Every choice already gives \(y=45\) at \(x=0\), so use the other two: \(-36+72+45=81\) at \(x=6\), and \(-225+180+45=0\) at \(x=15\). Only B passes both.

whyWrong.C: It works at \(x=6\) (\(36+45=81\)) but at \(x=15\) it gives \(225+45=270\), not 0. Testing only one extra point is what makes this trap work.

stem:
\[ \frac{1}{x}+\frac{1}{x-3}=\frac{6}{x^2-3x} \]
What are all the solutions to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Factor the right denominator: \(x^2-3x=x(x-3)\), which is the common denominator of the two fractions on the left. Multiply every term by \(x(x-3)\) and the quadratic disappears: \((x-3)+x=6\), so \(2x=9\) and \(x=\frac{9}{2}\). It is neither 0 nor 3, so it is allowed.

whyWrong.A: Neither value works. At \(x=6\) the left side is \(\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{3}=\frac{1}{2}\) while the right side is \(\frac{6}{18}=\frac{1}{3}\).
whyWrong.B: 0 and 3 are exactly the values that make the denominators zero, so they are excluded from the domain rather than solutions.
whyWrong.C: \(x=3\) makes \(x-3=0\); the equation is undefined there.

stem:
\[ x^2-2x-18=0 \]
One solution to the given equation can be written as \(1+\sqrt{k}\), where \(k\) is a constant. What is the value of \(k\) ?
whyCorrect: Complete the square: \(x^2-2x=18\) becomes \((x-1)^2=18+1=19\), so \(x=1\pm\sqrt{19}\) and \(k=19\). The quadratic formula gives the same thing: \(\frac{2\pm\sqrt{76}}{2}=1\pm\sqrt{19}\), because \(\sqrt{76}=2\sqrt{19}\).

whyWrong.A: 17 comes from subtracting 1 when completing the square instead of adding it. You add \(\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2=1\) to both sides.
whyWrong.C: 38 is half of the discriminant 76. Halving under the radical is not the same as dividing the whole root by 2 — you have to pull a factor of \(\sqrt{4}\) out first.
whyWrong.D: 76 is the discriminant \(b^2-4ac\) itself, before dividing by \(2a\).

stem: For a certain type of rope, the equation \(y=900ax^2\), where \(a\) is a constant, gives the estimated breaking strength \(y\), in pounds, of a rope with a circumference of \(x\) inches. Based on this equation, if a rope of this type has a circumference of 2.75 inches, it has an estimated breaking strength of 9,528.75 pounds. What is the estimated breaking strength, in pounds, of a rope of this type that has a circumference of 7.50 inches?
whyCorrect: Treat \(900a\) as one unknown constant. From the given rope, \(900a(2.75)^2=9528.75\), and \((2.75)^2=7.5625\), so \(900a=\frac{9528.75}{7.5625}=1260\). Then for \(x=7.5\): \(y=1260(7.5)^2=1260(56.25)=70{,}875\). Do not scale the strength by \(\frac{7.5}{2.75}\) — the relationship is squared.

stem:
\[ 4x^2+21=48+r \]
In the given equation, \(r\) is a constant. The equation has exactly one real solution. What is the value of \(r\) ?
whyCorrect: Isolate the squared term: \(4x^2=27+r\), so \(x^2=\frac{27+r}{4}\). A squared quantity equal to a positive number gives two solutions and equal to a negative number gives none, so exactly one solution requires \(27+r=0\), i.e. \(r=-27\) (and then \(x=0\)).

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=ax^2+bx+c\), where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are constants. The graph of \(y=f(x)\) in the \(xy\)-plane passes through the points \((10,0)\) and \((-5,0)\). If \(a\) is an integer greater than 1, which of the following could be the value of \(a+b\) ?
whyCorrect: The two points are the \(x\)-intercepts, so \(f(x)=a(x-10)(x+5)=a(x^2-5x-50)\). That makes \(b=-5a\), so \(a+b=a-5a=-4a\). With \(a\) an integer greater than 1, \(a+b\) is \(-8, -12, -16,\dots\); \(a=2\) gives \(-8\).

whyWrong.B: \(-4\) needs \(a=1\), which the stem rules out.
whyWrong.C: \(a+b=-4a\) is negative for every allowed \(a\), so no positive value is possible. 5 looks like the sum of the intercepts read with the wrong signs.
whyWrong.D: Also positive, so impossible; and it is not a multiple of 4, which every value of \(-4a\) must be.

note: All four answer choices are printed with the label "A)" in the book. Transcribed here as A-D in the printed order (-8, -4, 5, 6).

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((w+7)(3w-10)\) ?
whyCorrect: Multiply every pair of terms: \(w\cdot 3w=3w^2\), \(w\cdot(-10)=-10w\), \(7\cdot 3w=21w\), \(7\cdot(-10)=-70\). The two middle terms combine: \(-10w+21w=11w\), giving \(3w^2+11w-70\).

whyWrong.A: \(4w^2\) comes from adding the coefficients \(1+3\) instead of multiplying them, and the constant \(-3\) from adding \(7+(-10)\).
whyWrong.B: Same adding-instead-of-multiplying error on both the leading and constant terms.
whyWrong.D: The leading and constant terms are right, but only one of the two middle products was used: \(21w\) without the \(-10w\).

stem: If \(\left(\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{33}{2}\right)^2-64=0\), what is the value of \((x-33)^2\) ?
whyCorrect: Notice that \(\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{33}{2}=\frac{x-33}{2}\). So the equation says \(\frac{(x-33)^2}{4}=64\), and multiplying both sides by 4 gives \((x-33)^2=256\). You never have to find \(x\).

whyWrong.A: 8 is \(\sqrt{64}\), the value of \(\frac{x-33}{2}\), not of \((x-33)^2\).
whyWrong.B: 33 is a constant lifted straight out of the equation.
whyWrong.C: 128 doubles 64 instead of multiplying by 4. The factor is \(2^2\) because the halving is inside a square.

stem:
\[ 2x^2-12x-13=0 \]
One solution to the given equation can be written as \(h-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{k}\), where \(h\) and \(k\) are integer constants. What is the value of \(h+k\) ?
whyCorrect: By the quadratic formula, \(x=\frac{12\pm\sqrt{144+104}}{4}=\frac{12\pm\sqrt{248}}{4}\). Simplify the radical before matching the form: \(\sqrt{248}=2\sqrt{62}\), so \(x=3\pm\frac{\sqrt{62}}{2}=3\pm\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{62}\). That gives \(h=3\), \(k=62\), and \(h+k=65\).

whyWrong.A: 13 is the constant term of the equation; \(k\) is the simplified radicand, not \(c\).
whyWrong.B: With \(h=3\) this needs \(k=11\), and \(\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{11}\approx 1.66\), while the actual offset from 3 is \(\approx 3.94\).
whyWrong.C: 31 is \(\frac{248}{8}\) — the radicand halved once too often. Pulling \(\sqrt{4}\) out of \(\sqrt{248}\) divides the radicand by 4, giving 62.

stem: The function \(f(x)=\frac{1}{9}(x-6)^2+3\) gives a toy car’s height above the ground \(f(x)\), in inches, \(x\) seconds after it started moving on an elevated track, where \(0\le x\le 10\). Which of the following is the best interpretation of the vertex of the graph of \(y=f(x)\) in the \(xy\)-plane?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The toy car’s minimum height was 3 inches above the ground.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The toy car’s minimum height was 6 inches above the ground.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The toy car’s height was 3 inches above the ground when it started moving.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The toy car’s height was 6 inches above the ground when it started moving.

whyCorrect: In vertex form \(a(x-h)^2+k\) the vertex is \((6,3)\), so 6 is a time and 3 is a height. The coefficient \(\frac{1}{9}\) is positive, so the parabola opens upward and the vertex is the lowest point: the minimum height is 3 inches, reached 6 seconds in.

whyWrong.B: 6 is the time in seconds at which the minimum occurs, not the height.
whyWrong.C: “When it started moving” is \(x=0\), and \(f(0)=\frac{36}{9}+3=7\) inches, not 3.
whyWrong.D: Both numbers are misread: 6 is a time, and the starting height is 7 inches.

stem:
\[ \frac{1}{cx}=\frac{x}{148}+\frac{1}{c} \]
In the given equation, \(c\) is a constant. If the equation has only one solution, what is the value of \(c\) ?
whyCorrect: Multiply every term by \(148cx\) to clear the fractions: the left side becomes 148 and the right becomes \(cx^2+148x\), so \(cx^2+148x-148=0\). One solution means the discriminant is zero: \(148^2-4(c)(-148)=0\), so \(21904+592c=0\) and \(c=-37\). (\(c\) cannot be 0, since \(\frac{1}{cx}\) would be undefined.)

stem:
\[ x^2=(40)(40) \]
What is the positive solution to the given equation?
whyCorrect: The right side is \(40^2=1600\), so \(x=\pm 40\) and the positive solution is 40. You do not need to multiply out — a square equal to \(40^2\) has \(\pm 40\) as its solutions.

stem:
y = 4x + 12
\(y=(x+2)^2\)

A solution to the given system of equations is \((x,y)\). What is the value of \(x^2\) ?
whyCorrect: Set the two expressions for \(y\) equal: \((x+2)^2=4x+12\). Expanding gives \(x^2+4x+4=4x+12\); the \(4x\) terms cancel, leaving \(x^2=8\). The question asks for \(x^2\), so you can stop there rather than taking a square root.

stem:
\[ f(x)=-9x^2+113x \]
The function \(f\) models the depth below sea level, in meters, of a certain seal \(x\) minutes after the seal dives into the water. What is the best interpretation of \(f(2)=190\) in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: 190 minutes after the seal dives into the water, its estimated depth is 2 meters below sea level.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The seal reaches an estimated maximum depth of 190 meters below sea level.

choices.label: C
choices.content: 2 minutes after the seal dives into the water, its estimated depth is 190 meters below the sea level.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Approximately 2 minutes after diving into the water, the seal returns to sea level.

whyCorrect: The input \(x\) is minutes and the output is depth in meters, so \(f(2)=190\) says: at 2 minutes, the depth is 190 meters. Read the number in the parentheses as the time and the number after the equals sign as the depth.

whyWrong.A: The 2 and the 190 are swapped.
whyWrong.B: A maximum requires the vertex, at \(x=\frac{113}{18}\approx 6.3\) minutes; the depth there is about 355 meters, not 190.
whyWrong.D: Returning to sea level means \(f(x)=0\), which happens at \(x=\frac{113}{9}\approx 12.6\) minutes, not at \(f(x)=190\).

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((x^2+11)^2+(x-8)(x+8)\) ?
whyCorrect: Expand each piece separately. \((x^2+11)^2=x^4+22x^2+121\) — the middle term is \(2\cdot 11\cdot x^2\), not zero. \((x-8)(x+8)=x^2-64\). Adding: \(x^4+(22+1)x^2+(121-64)=x^4+23x^2+57\).

whyWrong.A: This drops the \(22x^2\) middle term and adds 64 instead of subtracting it (\(121+64=185\)).
whyWrong.B: The middle term is wrong and the second product has been ignored entirely; 121 alone is the constant from the first square.
whyWrong.C: The \(x^2\) term is right, but the constant subtracts 64 from 11 rather than from 121.

stem:
\[ x^2+2x=72 \]
What is one of the solutions to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Complete the square: \(x^2+2x+1=72+1\), so \((x+1)^2=73\) and \(x=-1\pm\sqrt{73}\). The 1 you add to complete the square also goes onto the right side, which is why the radicand is 73 and not 71.

whyWrong.A: The radicand is right but the sign is not: \((x+1)^2\) gives \(x=-1\pm\sqrt{73}\), not \(+1\).
whyWrong.B: Both parts are wrong — the sign, and a radicand of 71 from subtracting 1 from 72 instead of adding.
whyWrong.D: Correct sign, but 71 comes from subtracting the completing-the-square constant instead of adding it.

stem: Which of the following expressions has a factor of \(x+2b\), where \(b\) is a positive integer constant?
whyCorrect: If \(x+2b\) is a factor, the other factor must be \(3x+c\) so the leading term is \(3x^2\). Expanding, \((x+2b)(3x+c)=3x^2+(c+6b)x+2bc\). Matching the constant \(2bc=14b\) forces \(c=7\), so the middle coefficient must be \(7+6b\). Only 25 fits a positive integer: \(b=3\), and \((x+6)(3x+7)=3x^2+25x+42\).

whyWrong.A: \(7+6b=7\) needs \(b=0\), and the stem says \(b\) is positive.
whyWrong.B: \(7+6b=16\) gives \(b=1.5\), not an integer.
whyWrong.C: \(7+6b=18\) gives \(b=\frac{11}{6}\), not an integer.

stem: The graph of a system of a linear equation and a quadratic equation is shown. A solution to the system is \((x,y)\). What is a possible value of \(x\) ?
whyCorrect: A solution to a system is a point where the two graphs cross, so read off the \(x\)-coordinates of the intersection points, not anything about a single curve. The horizontal line meets the parabola at \(x=4\) and \(x=6\); of those, only 4 is offered.

whyWrong.B: 5 is where the parabola peaks. The vertex is above the line, so it is not an intersection point.
whyWrong.C: 6.4 is the \(y\)-value of the horizontal line, not an \(x\)-coordinate.
whyWrong.D: At \(x=7\) the parabola is below the line; the second crossing is at \(x=6\).

note: Depends on the printed graph (a downward parabola with x-intercepts 2 and 8 and a horizontal line just above y = 6), which cannot be reproduced as a table. The last two choices are both printed with the label "C)"; transcribed here as C and D in printed order.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(13(x^2-7)\) ?
whyCorrect: Distribute the 13 to both terms inside the parentheses: \(13\cdot x^2=13x^2\) and \(13\cdot(-7)=-91\).

whyWrong.B: \(-20\) comes from \(-13-7\), subtracting instead of multiplying.
whyWrong.C: The 13 was distributed only to the first term; the \(-7\) must be multiplied too.
whyWrong.D: \(+6\) comes from \(13-7\), adding instead of multiplying, and it also loses the negative sign.

stem: Which quadratic equation has no real solution?
whyCorrect: Check the discriminant \(b^2-4ac\) for each. For D, \(a=-2\), \(b=2\), \(c=-2\), so \(b^2-4ac=4-4(-2)(-2)=4-16=-12\), which is negative, so there is no real solution. The two negatives in \(-4ac\) multiply to a positive and get subtracted — that is what makes this one different.

whyWrong.A: \(-2x^2=0\) gives \(x=0\), one real solution.
whyWrong.B: \(x^2=1\), so \(x=\pm 1\), two real solutions.
whyWrong.C: Factor: \(-2x(x-1)=0\), so \(x=0\) or \(x=1\), two real solutions.

stem:
\[ 21x^2+(21s+r)x+rs=0 \]
In the given equation, \(r\) and \(s\) are positive constants. The product of the solutions to the given equation is \(krs\), where \(k\) is a constant. What is the value of \(k\) ?
whyCorrect: For \(ax^2+bx+c=0\), the product of the solutions is \(\frac{c}{a}\). Here that is \(\frac{rs}{21}=\frac{1}{21}rs\), so \(k=\frac{1}{21}\). Factoring confirms it: \((21x+r)(x+s)=0\) has solutions \(-\frac{r}{21}\) and \(-s\), whose product is \(\frac{rs}{21}\).

stem:
\[ -16(5x-3)^2+4(5x-2)^2 \]
The given expression can be rewritten as \(\frac{a}{4}x^2+\frac{b}{4}x+\frac{c}{4}\), where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are constants. What is the value of \(a+b+c\) ?

whyWrong.B: \(-56\) is twice \(-28\) — the coefficients were doubled instead of multiplied by 4.
whyWrong.C: \(-28\) is \(-300+400-128\), the sum of the coefficients themselves. Each one is \(\frac{a}{4}\), not \(a\), so all three must be multiplied by 4.
whyWrong.D: \(-7\) divides the coefficient sum by 4 instead of multiplying by it — the correction is applied the wrong way round.

stem: The graph of a system of a linear equation and a quadratic equation is shown. Which of the following is a solution \((x,y)\) to the system?
whyCorrect: A solution to a system has to lie on both graphs at once, which means an intersection point. The line and the parabola cross at the labeled point \((-1,4)\).

whyWrong.B: \((0,0)\) is the vertex of the parabola only. The line passes above it at \(x=0\), so the point is not on both graphs.
whyWrong.C: \((0,9)\) is on neither graph — the line crosses the \(y\)-axis at 8 and the parabola at 0.
whyWrong.D: This choice is missing from the printed book.

note: Choice D is blank in the book (the label "D)" is printed with no text). The graph is required: a parabola with vertex at the origin and a line through (-1,4) with y-intercept 8, intersecting at (-1,4).

stem: If \(121x^2=-110x+56\), what is the value of 11x + 5, where 11x + 5 > 0 ?
whyCorrect: Move everything but the constant to the left: \(121x^2+110x=56\). The left side is one step from a perfect square, since \((11x+5)^2=121x^2+110x+25\). Add 25 to both sides: \((11x+5)^2=81\), so \(11x+5=\pm 9\), and the condition \(11x+5>0\) picks 9.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=4x^2\). What is the value of \(f(11)\) ?
whyCorrect: Square first, then multiply: \(f(11)=4(11)^2=4\cdot 121=484\). The exponent applies only to \(x\), so you cannot multiply the 4 and the 11 before squaring.

whyWrong.A: 44 is \(4\cdot 11\) with the squaring left out.
whyWrong.B: 52 has no route from the function; it looks like a stray sum.
whyWrong.C: 88 is \(4\cdot 11\cdot 2\) — doubling instead of squaring.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(2\left(x-\frac{3}{2}\right)(x+14)\) ?
whyCorrect: Multiply the 2 into the first bracket to clear the fraction: \(2\left(x-\frac{3}{2}\right)=2x-3\). Then \((2x-3)(x+14)=2x^2+28x-3x-42=2x^2+25x-42\).

whyWrong.A: The 2 was used only to cancel the fraction and never multiplied through, so the leading coefficient and the constant are both half of what they should be.
whyWrong.B: The middle term \(14-3=11\) mixes the 14 from one bracket with the 3 from the other without multiplying by 2; the constant is also missing its factor of 2.
whyWrong.D: Both middle products were dropped. \(2x\cdot 14\) and \(-3\cdot x\) still have to be added.

stem:
\[ -8x(x+9)=40 \]
One solution to the given equation can be written as \(x=-\frac{s+\sqrt{t}}{2}\), where \(s\) and \(t\) are positive integers. What is the value of \(\frac{s}{t}\) ?
whyCorrect: Expand and divide by \(-8\) first, which keeps the numbers small: \(-8x^2-72x=40\) becomes \(x^2+9x+5=0\). Then \(x=\frac{-9\pm\sqrt{81-20}}{2}=\frac{-9\pm\sqrt{61}}{2}\), and the solution matching \(-\frac{s+\sqrt{t}}{2}\) has \(s=9\), \(t=61\), so \(\frac{s}{t}=\frac{9}{61}\).

whyWrong.A: 101 comes from \(81+20\); the discriminant subtracts \(4ac\), and here \(c=+5\) so 20 is subtracted.
whyWrong.B: 76 comes from \(81-5\), using \(c\) instead of \(4ac\). The \(4a\) factor matters: \(4(1)(5)=20\).
whyWrong.D: \(s=18\) doubles the 9. In \(\frac{-9\pm\sqrt{61}}{2}\) the 9 is already the numerator, so there is nothing to clear.

stem:
\[ x(x+4)-140=3x(x-10) \]
What is the sum of the solutions to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Expand both sides: \(x^2+4x-140=3x^2-30x\). Collect everything on one side: \(2x^2-34x+140=0\), and dividing by 2 gives \(x^2-17x+70=0\). The sum of the solutions is \(-\frac{b}{a}=17\) (the roots are 7 and 10).

whyWrong.A: 6 is \(10-4\), read straight off the numbers in the stem rather than from the collected equation.
whyWrong.B: 10 is only one of the two solutions; the question asks for their sum.
whyWrong.C: 14 is \(10+4\), again the stem's numbers rather than the roots. The 4 and the 10 are inside brackets that get multiplied out, so they are not the roots.

stem:
\[ -3x^2-7x+1=0 \]
What is the greatest solution to the given equation?
whyCorrect: Multiply through by \(-1\) so the leading coefficient is positive: \(3x^2+7x-1=0\). Then \(x=\frac{-7\pm\sqrt{49+12}}{6}=-\frac{7}{6}\pm\frac{\sqrt{61}}{6}\), and the greatest solution takes the plus sign.

whyWrong.A: The denominator is \(2a=6\), not 3. Using \(a\) instead of \(2a\) doubles both terms.
whyWrong.B: Same denominator error, and it takes the smaller root as well.
whyWrong.D: Correct denominators but the minus sign, which gives the smaller of the two solutions.

stem:
\[ x(13x+27)+c=5 \]
In the given equation, \(c\) is a constant. A solution to the equation is \(-\frac{27+\sqrt{261}}{26}\). What is the value of \(c\) ?
whyCorrect: Put the equation in standard form: \(13x^2+27x+(c-5)=0\). The quadratic formula gives \(x=\frac{-27\pm\sqrt{729-52(c-5)}}{26}\), and the denominator 26 already matches, so the radicands must match: \(729-52c+260=261\). That gives \(52c=728\) and \(c=14\).

stem: If \(\frac{g}{h} = \frac{1}{100}\) and \(\frac{10g}{kh} = \frac{1}{100}\), what is the value of \(k\)?
whyCorrect: Pull the constants out of the second fraction: \(\frac{10g}{kh}=\frac{10}{k}\cdot\frac{g}{h}\). Substituting \(\frac{g}{h}=\frac{1}{100}\) gives \(\frac{10}{k}\cdot\frac{1}{100}=\frac{1}{100}\), so \(\frac{10}{k}=1\) and \(k=10\). The whole point is that the two fractions are equal, so the extra factor of 10 on top must be cancelled by a 10 on the bottom.

whyWrong.A: 0.1 is \(\frac{1}{10}\); you divided by 10 where you should have multiplied, i.e. solved \(10k=1\).
whyWrong.C: 100 comes from copying the denominator of \(\frac{1}{100}\) instead of comparing the two equations.
whyWrong.D: 1,000 is \(10\times 100\); you multiplied the 10 in the numerator by the 100 instead of cancelling it.

stem: Julia purchased 600 feet of fencing. She used 70% of this fencing to surround a vegetable garden. How many feet of fencing did Julia use to surround the vegetable garden?
whyCorrect: 70% of 600 is 0.70 × 600 = 420 feet. Convert the percent to a decimal and multiply by the total; do not divide.

whyWrong.A: 14 is \(\frac{700}{50}\)-type arithmetic, or 600 divided by roughly 43; dividing by the percent instead of multiplying by it.
whyWrong.B: 35 is half of 70. You worked with the percent number itself rather than applying it to 600.
whyWrong.D: 530 is 600 − 70; you subtracted the percent as if it were a number of feet.

stem: If \(\frac{2a}{b} = 5.8\) and \(\frac{a}{bn} = 23.2\), what is the value of \(\frac{1}{n}\)?
whyCorrect: From the first equation \(\frac{a}{b}=\frac{5.8}{2}=2.9\). The second equation is \(\frac{a}{b}\cdot\frac{1}{n}=23.2\), so \(2.9\cdot\frac{1}{n}=23.2\) and \(\frac{1}{n}=\frac{23.2}{2.9}=8\). The step people miss is halving 5.8 first — the first equation gives \(\frac{2a}{b}\), not \(\frac{a}{b}\).

stem: After 20% of the original number of objects in a group were removed from the group, 180 objects remained in the group. How many objects were removed from the group?
whyCorrect: The 180 that remain are the other 80%, not the whole group. So \(0.80x=180\) gives an original \(x=225\), and the number removed is \(225-180=45\) (or 20% of 225).

whyWrong.A: 36 is 20% of 180. That treats 180 as the original group, but 180 is what was left after the removal.
whyWrong.C: 225 is the original number of objects, not the number removed. The question asks how many were taken out.
whyWrong.D: 900 comes from dividing 180 by 0.20 instead of by 0.80 — that is the size of a group whose 20% is 180.

stem: A company studied a random sample of 20 lawns in a small town. The company found that 4 of these lawns contain fertilizer. If there are 260 lawns in the town, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of lawns that contain fertilizer?
whyCorrect: The sample rate is \(\frac{4}{20}=0.2\), so apply that rate to the whole town: 0.2 × 260 = 52 lawns. Set it up as the proportion \(\frac{4}{20}=\frac{n}{260}\) if you prefer.

whyWrong.A: 3 is close to \(\frac{260}{...}\) nothing meaningful; it is far too small — a fifth of 260 cannot be a single-digit number.
whyWrong.B: 5 is \(\frac{20}{4}\), the reciprocal of the rate rather than the rate applied to 260.
whyWrong.C: 13 is \(\frac{260}{20}\) — the number of sample-sized groups in the town, not the number of fertilized lawns. You still have to multiply that by 4.

stem: Each side of square \(A\) has a length of 24 inches. Each side of square \(A\) is multiplied by a scale factor of 2 to create square \(B\). What is the length, in inches, of each side of square \(B\)?
whyCorrect: A scale factor multiplies the side length: 24 × 2 = 48 inches. A scale factor is never added or subtracted.

whyWrong.A: 22 is \(24-2\); you subtracted the scale factor instead of multiplying by it.
whyWrong.B: 24 is the original side length, unchanged. The square was scaled, so it cannot stay the same.
whyWrong.C: 26 is \(24+2\); you added the scale factor instead of multiplying by it.

stem: The mass of object A is 483% of the mass of object B, and the mass of object A is 0.069% of the mass of object C. If the mass of object C is \(p\)% of the mass of object B, what is the value of \(\frac{p}{1{,}000}\)?
whyCorrect: Write both statements with decimals: \(A = 4.83B\) and \(A = 0.00069C\). Setting them equal gives \(0.00069C = 4.83B\), so \(C = \frac{4.83}{0.00069}B = 7{,}000B\). C is therefore 700,000% of B, so \(p = 700{,}000\) and \(\frac{p}{1{,}000} = 700\). The step people drop is the last one — converting the multiplier 7,000 into a percent by multiplying by 100 before dividing by 1,000.

stem: The mass of object A is 416% of the mass of object B, and the mass of object A is 0.064% of the mass of object C. If the mass of object C is \(p\)% of the mass of object B, what is the value of \(\frac{p}{1{,}000}\)?
whyCorrect: In decimals, \(A = 4.16B\) and \(A = 0.00064C\). Equating them, \(C = \frac{4.16}{0.00064}B = 6{,}500B\), so C is 650,000% of B. That makes \(p = 650{,}000\) and \(\frac{p}{1{,}000} = 650\). Convert every percent to a decimal first; trying to work with the percent signs in place is where this goes wrong.

stem: Julia purchased 800 feet of fencing. She used 60% of this fencing to surround a vegetable garden. How many feet of fencing did Julia use to surround a vegetable garden?
whyCorrect: 60% of 800 is 0.60 × 800 = 480 feet. Turn the percent into a decimal and multiply by the total amount.

whyWrong.A: 12 comes from dividing rather than multiplying (800 ÷ 60 ≈ 13); the answer must be a large share of 800.
whyWrong.B: 30 is half of 60. You worked with the percent number itself instead of applying it to 800.
whyWrong.D: 740 is 800 − 60; you subtracted the percent as though it were a number of feet.

stem: Jasmin grows bean pods in her garden. This year, she harvested 330 bean pods and saved 10% of them to plant next year. How many of the harvested bean pods did Jasmin save to plant next year?
whyCorrect: 10% of a number is that number divided by 10: \(330 \div 10 = 33\). Equivalently 0.10 × 330 = 33.

whyWrong.A: 23 is \(33-10\); you found 10% and then subtracted 10 again.
whyWrong.C: 41 does not follow from any correct step here; 10% of 330 must end in a 3 because 330 divided by 10 is exact.
whyWrong.D: 43 is \(33+10\), adding the percent number on top of the correct answer.

stem: In a collection of items, 10% are red, 25% are green, 35% are blue, and 30% are yellow. If there are 40 green items, how many blue items are in the collection?
whyCorrect: You cannot go from green to blue directly — find the total first. Green is 25% of the collection, so \(0.25T = 40\) gives \(T = 160\). Blue is 35% of that: 0.35 × 160 = 56.

whyWrong.A: 14 is 35% of 40. That treats the 40 green items as the whole collection instead of a quarter of it.
whyWrong.B: 16 is 40% of 40, again applying a percent to the green count rather than to the total.
whyWrong.C: 48 is 30% of 160 — the yellow items. You used the wrong percent from the list.

stem: If 350% of \(n\) is 35, what is the value of \(n\)?
whyCorrect: 350% means 3.5, so the equation is \(3.5n = 35\) and \(n = 10\). Because the percent is above 100, \(n\) has to be smaller than 35 — that alone eliminates the three large choices.

whyWrong.A: 12,250 is 350 × 35; you multiplied instead of dividing and never converted the percent to a decimal.
whyWrong.B: 1,225 is \(35^{2}\), which no step of this problem produces.
whyWrong.C: 1,000 comes from mishandling the \(\div 100\) in the percent conversion, dividing 35 by 0.035 instead of 3.5.

stem: In a random sample of 276 residents in a certain building, 9 residents reported that they take the train to work. If there are a total of 1,380 residents in this building, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of building residents who take the train to work?
whyCorrect: Scale the sample up to the building. The building has \(\frac{1{,}380}{276}=5\) times as many residents as the sample, so multiply the 9 train riders by 5 to get 45. As a proportion: \(\frac{9}{276}=\frac{n}{1{,}380}\).

whyWrong.A: 9 is the count in the 276-person sample. The building is five times larger, so the estimate must be larger too.
whyWrong.C: 276 is the sample size, not a count of train riders.
whyWrong.D: 1,095 is \(1{,}380-285\)-style arithmetic; it would mean about 79% of residents take the train, when the sample rate is only about 3%.

stem: The result of increasing the quantity \(x\) by 600% is 126. What is the value of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Increasing by 600% means adding 6 times the original to the original, so the result is \(x + 6x = 7x\), not \(6x\). From \(7x = 126\) you get \(x = 18\).

whyWrong.B: 21 is \(\frac{126}{6}\). That treats "increased by 600%" as "is 600% of", forgetting that the original quantity is still there.
whyWrong.C: 474 is \(126 \times 6 - 282\)-type arithmetic; more simply, it comes from working backwards with subtraction. Increasing \(x\) must make it bigger, so \(x\) has to be smaller than 126.
whyWrong.D: 756 is \(126 \times 6\); you multiplied when the 126 is already the increased amount.

stem: An object moves at a speed of \(\frac{3}{50}\) feet per second. What is this speed, in yards per second? (3 feet = 1 yard)
whyCorrect: A yard is bigger than a foot, so the number of yards must be smaller: divide by 3. \(\frac{3}{50} \div 3 = \frac{1}{50}\) yards per second.

whyWrong.A: 50 is the denominator flipped up; no step here produces a whole number that large.
whyWrong.B: 6 comes from ignoring the fraction entirely and treating the speed as some multiple of 3.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{9}{50}\) is \(\frac{3}{50} \times 3\). You multiplied by the conversion factor when converting to the larger unit requires dividing.

stem: At a convention center, there are a total of 325 visitors. Each visitor is located in either room \(A\), room \(B\), or room \(C\). If one of these visitors is selected at random, the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room \(A\) is 0.48, and the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room \(B\) is 0.16. How many visitors are located in room \(C\)?
whyCorrect: Every visitor is in exactly one of the three rooms, so the three probabilities add to 1. That makes \(P(C) = 1 - 0.48 - 0.16 = 0.36\), and the count is 0.36 × 325 = 117.

whyWrong.A: 25 is close to \(325 \times 0.08\); it comes from subtracting the two probabilities from each other (0.48 − 0.16 = 0.32) and then mishandling the total.
whyWrong.B: 36 is the probability 0.36 read as a number of visitors. You still have to multiply by the 325 total.

stem: At a convention center, there are a total of 375 visitors. Each visitor is located in either room \(A\), room \(B\), or room \(C\). If one of these visitors is selected at random, the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room \(A\) is 0.48, and the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room \(B\) is 0.32. How many visitors are located in room \(C\)?
whyCorrect: The three room probabilities must total 1, so \(P(C) = 1 - 0.48 - 0.32 = 0.20\). Then 0.20 × 375 = 75 visitors.

whyWrong.A: 20 is the percentage 20% written as a count. Multiply that probability by the 375 total.
whyWrong.B: 58 comes from taking 0.48 − 0.32 = 0.16 and then applying it inconsistently; the complement, not the difference, gives room C.
whyWrong.C: 60 is \(0.16 \times 375\), using the difference between the two given probabilities instead of what is left over from 1.

stem: At a convention center, there are a total of 275 visitors. Each visitor is located in either room \(A\), room \(B\), or room \(C\). If one of these visitors is selected at random, the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room \(A\) is 0.68, and the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room \(B\) is 0.24. How many visitors are located in room \(C\)?
whyCorrect: Rooms A, B and C cover everyone, so their probabilities sum to 1: \(P(C) = 1 - 0.68 - 0.24 = 0.08\). The count is 0.08 × 275 = 22.

whyWrong.A: 8 is the probability 0.08 expressed as a percent and then read as a count of visitors.
whyWrong.C: 45 is roughly \(0.44 \times ...\); it comes from using the difference 0.68 − 0.24 = 0.44 in place of the complement, then mis-scaling.
whyWrong.D: 121 is \(0.44 \times 275\), the difference of the two given probabilities rather than what remains after both are removed from 1.

stem: At a convention center, there are a total of 375 visitors. Each visitor is located in either room \(A\), room \(B\), or room \(C\). If one of these visitors is selected at random, the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room \(A\) is 0.48, and the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room \(B\) is 0.24. How many visitors are located in room \(C\)?
whyCorrect: Since every visitor is in exactly one room, \(P(C) = 1 - 0.48 - 0.24 = 0.28\), so room C holds 0.28 × 375 = 105 visitors.

whyWrong.A: 28 is the probability 0.28 read straight off as a count; it still has to be multiplied by 375.
whyWrong.B: 43 does not come from any correct step — it is roughly the count you would get from a 0.115 probability.
whyWrong.C: 90 is \(0.24 \times 375\), the number of visitors in room B rather than room C.

stem: At a convention center, there are a total of 375 visitors. Each visitor is located in either room \(A\), room \(B\), or room \(C\). If one of these visitors is selected at random, the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room \(A\) is 0.68, and the probability of selecting a visitor who is located in room \(B\) is 0.24. How many visitors are located in room \(C\)?
whyCorrect: The three rooms account for every visitor, so their probabilities add to 1: \(P(C) = 1 - 0.68 - 0.24 = 0.08\). Multiply by the total: 0.08 × 375 = 30.

whyWrong.A: 8 is the probability 0.08 written as a percent and mistaken for a count of visitors.
whyWrong.C: 61 is not produced by any correct step; it is roughly 16% of 375, which is neither the complement nor the difference.

stem: Which of the following expressions is equivalent to \(\left(\frac{a}{4} + \frac{b}{3}\right)^{2}\)?
whyCorrect: Use \((m+n)^{2} = m^{2} + 2mn + n^{2}\) with \(m = \frac{a}{4}\) and \(n = \frac{b}{3}\). The squares are \(\frac{a^{2}}{16}\) and \(\frac{b^{2}}{9}\), and the middle term is \(2 \cdot \frac{a}{4} \cdot \frac{b}{3} = \frac{2ab}{12} = \frac{ab}{6}\). Squaring the denominators and remembering the factor of 2 are the two steps that get dropped.

whyWrong.A: This squares the numerators but leaves the denominators alone and drops the middle term entirely.
whyWrong.B: The squares are right, but a binomial squared always has a cross term \(2mn\); it is missing here.
whyWrong.C: The cross term \(\frac{ab}{12}\) omits the factor of 2, and the denominators 4 and 3 were not squared.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((3x^{3} - x^{2} + 4)(5x^{2} + 8x)\)?
whyCorrect: Distribute every term: \(3x^{3}(5x^{2}+8x) = 15x^{5} + 24x^{4}\), \(-x^{2}(5x^{2}+8x) = -5x^{4} - 8x^{3}\), and \(4(5x^{2}+8x) = 20x^{2} + 32x\). Combining \(24x^{4} - 5x^{4}\) gives \(19x^{4}\), leaving \(15x^{5} + 19x^{4} - 8x^{3} + 20x^{2} + 32x\). Note that every term of the second factor has an \(x\), so the product cannot have a constant term.

whyWrong.A: The last two terms have lost a power of \(x\); \(4 \cdot 5x^{2} = 20x^{2}\), not \(20x\), and \(4 \cdot 8x = 32x\), not 32.
whyWrong.B: The \(20x^{2}\) term is negative here, but it comes from \(+4 \cdot 5x^{2}\), and the constant 32 again drops an \(x\).
whyWrong.D: \(29x^{4}\) comes from adding \(24x^{4} + 5x^{4}\) instead of subtracting; the \(-x^{2}\) term makes that contribution negative.

stem: If \(\frac{6}{7}p + 12 = 54\), what is the value of \(7p\)?
whyCorrect: Subtract 12: \(\frac{6}{7}p = 42\). Multiply both sides by \(\frac{7}{6}\): \(p = 49\). The question asks for \(7p\), so the answer is \(7 \times 49 = 343\) — read the last line before you stop at \(p\).

stem: \[b^{2} + 5c = 9d\]The given equation relates the real numbers \(b\), \(c\), and \(d\), where \(d > \frac{5}{9}c\). Which equation correctly expresses \(b\) in terms of \(c\) and \(d\)?
whyCorrect: Isolate \(b^{2}\) by subtracting \(5c\): \(b^{2} = 9d - 5c\). Undoing a square means taking a square root, not dividing by 2, and both signs are possible: \(b = \pm\sqrt{9d - 5c}\). The condition \(d > \frac{5}{9}c\) is there to guarantee \(9d - 5c > 0\) so the root is real.

whyWrong.A: Dividing by 2 undoes multiplication by 2, not squaring; the \(5c\) also has to be subtracted, not added.
whyWrong.B: Same error — \(b^{2}\) becomes \(b\) by a square root, not by halving.
whyWrong.C: The sign is wrong: moving \(+5c\) to the other side makes it \(-5c\). With \(+5c\) the given restriction on \(d\) would serve no purpose.

whyCorrect: Do not solve for \(x\) and \(y\). Recognise \(x^{6} - y^{6}\) as a difference of squares of \(x^{3}\) and \(y^{3}\): \(x^{6} - y^{6} = (x^{3} + y^{3})(x^{3} - y^{3}) = 12 \times 6 = 72\).

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(2(xy^{2} + x^{2}y) - 8(xy^{2} - 4x^{2}y)\)?
whyCorrect: Distribute both coefficients, keeping the sign on the second: \(2xy^{2} + 2x^{2}y - 8xy^{2} + 32x^{2}y\). The \(-8\) times \(-4x^{2}y\) is \(+32x^{2}y\). Combining like terms gives \(-6xy^{2} + 34x^{2}y\).

whyWrong.B: \(33x^{2}y\) uses \(32 + 1\); the first bracket contributes \(2x^{2}y\), not \(x^{2}y\).
whyWrong.C: \(-30x^{2}y\) comes from distributing \(-8\) over \(-4x^{2}y\) as \(-32x^{2}y\); two negatives multiply to a positive.
whyWrong.D: Same sign error on the \(32x^{2}y\) term, combined with using \(1x^{2}y\) instead of \(2x^{2}y\) from the first bracket.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((131y)^{\frac{1}{2}}\), where \(y > 1\)?
whyCorrect: An exponent of \(\frac{1}{2}\) is a square root, and the exponent applies to everything inside the parentheses. So \((131y)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{131y}\).

whyWrong.A: Here the root was applied only to \(y\), leaving 131 outside untouched. The 131 is inside the parentheses, so it is under the root too.
whyWrong.B: This roots only the 131 and leaves \(y\) outside — the same mistake in reverse.
whyWrong.D: Squaring inside and then taking the root returns \(131y\) itself (for positive values), which is the original expression, not its square root.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((5a^{2} - 3ab + 7b^{2}) - (4a^{2} + ab - 2b^{2})\)?
whyCorrect: The minus sign applies to every term in the second bracket: \(-4a^{2} - ab + 2b^{2}\). Now combine like terms: \(5a^{2}-4a^{2}=a^{2}\), \(-3ab-ab=-4ab\), \(7b^{2}+2b^{2}=9b^{2}\).

whyWrong.B: Here the minus was distributed only onto the first term. Subtracting \(+ab\) gives \(-4ab\), and subtracting \(-2b^{2}\) gives \(+9b^{2}\).
whyWrong.C: Adding and subtracting like terms never changes the exponents; \(a^{2}\) stays \(a^{2}\), it does not become \(a^{4}\).
whyWrong.D: Both errors at once: the exponents were doubled and the subtraction was not distributed across the whole bracket.

stem: \[7x + 16 = \frac{4}{y}\]The given equation relates the distinct positive numbers \(x\) and \(y\). Which equation correctly expresses \(y\) in terms of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \(y\): \(y(7x+16) = 4\). Then divide by \(7x+16\): \(y = \frac{4}{7x+16}\). The whole expression \(7x+16\) is the divisor, so it goes under the 4 as a single block.

whyWrong.A: This subtracts 4 from 16 as if \(\frac{4}{y}\) were \(4\); the \(y\) cannot simply be dropped.
whyWrong.C: This is the reciprocal of the correct answer — you solved for \(\frac{1}{y}\) and forgot to flip.
whyWrong.D: Multiplying by 4 instead of dividing; the 4 sits in the numerator of \(\frac{4}{y}\), so it ends up in the numerator of \(y\).

stem: \[v = -\frac{w}{130x}\]The given equation relates the distinct positive numbers \(v\), \(w\), and \(x\). Which equation correctly expresses \(w\) in terms of \(v\) and \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \(130x\) to clear the denominator: \(130xv = -w\). Then multiply by \(-1\), giving \(w = -130vx\). The \(x\) is in the denominator on the right, so it moves up to the left side as a factor.

whyWrong.B: This leaves \(x\) in the denominator. Since \(x\) divides \(w\) in the original equation, undoing that division multiplies by \(x\).
whyWrong.C: This inverts the whole expression — \(v\) ends up in the denominator, but \(v\) is by itself on the left, so it becomes a factor, not a divisor.
whyWrong.D: The original relationship is a product/quotient, not a sum; you cannot move \(130x\) across the equals sign by adding it.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(60y + 90y\)?
whyCorrect: These are like terms, so add the coefficients and keep the variable as it is: \(60y + 90y = 150y\). Adding terms never multiplies the variables together.

whyWrong.A: 540 is \(60 \times 9\) and the \(y^{2}\) comes from multiplying rather than adding — both wrong operations.
whyWrong.B: 540 comes from multiplying the coefficients instead of adding them.
whyWrong.C: The coefficient 150 is right, but adding \(y + y\) gives \(2y\), not \(y^{2}\); exponents only add when the terms are multiplied.

stem: If 9(x + 3) = 81, what is the value of x + 3?
whyCorrect: Treat \(x+3\) as a single block. Dividing both sides by 9 gives \(x + 3 = 9\) directly — there is no need to find \(x\) at all. (If you do, \(x = 6\), but the question asks for \(x+3\).)

whyWrong.A: 6 is the value of \(x\), not \(x+3\). Read the last line of the question.
whyWrong.C: 69 is \(81 - 12\)-style arithmetic; dividing by 9, not subtracting, undoes the multiplication.
whyWrong.D: 72 is \(81 - 9\), subtracting the 9 instead of dividing by it.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((9nr^{2} + 3nr) + (6n^{2}r + 5nr)\)?
whyCorrect: Only \(3nr\) and \(5nr\) are like terms; they combine to \(8nr\). \(9nr^{2}\) and \(6n^{2}r\) have different variable parts (\(nr^{2}\) versus \(n^{2}r\)), so neither can be combined with anything and both stay as they are.

whyWrong.A: This adds \(9nr^{2}\) and \(6n^{2}r\) as though they were like terms. \(nr^{2}\) and \(n^{2}r\) are different, so 9 and 6 cannot be added.
whyWrong.B: Same false combination, plus the exponents were multiplied together; adding terms never changes exponents.
whyWrong.C: 54 is \(9 \times 6\) and 15 is \(3 \times 5\) — the terms were multiplied instead of added.

stem: \[v = -\frac{w}{161x}\]The given equation relates the distinct positive numbers \(v\), \(w\), and \(x\). Which equation correctly expresses \(w\) in terms of \(v\) and \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \(161x\) to clear the denominator: \(161xv = -w\). Then multiply by \(-1\), giving \(w = -161vx\). The \(x\) is in the denominator on the right, so it moves up to the left side as a factor.

whyWrong.B: This leaves \(x\) in the denominator. Since \(x\) divides \(w\) in the original equation, undoing that division multiplies by \(x\).
whyWrong.C: This inverts the whole expression — \(v\) ends up in the denominator, but \(v\) is by itself on the left, so it becomes a factor, not a divisor.
whyWrong.D: The original relationship is a product/quotient, not a sum; you cannot move \(161x\) across the equals sign by adding it.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(\frac{y + 2}{x - 9} + \frac{y(x - 9)}{x^{2}y - 9xy}\)?
whyCorrect: Factor the second denominator first: \(x^{2}y - 9xy = xy(x-9)\), so the second fraction is \(\frac{y(x-9)}{xy(x-9)} = \frac{1}{x}\). Now add over the common denominator \(x(x-9)\): \(\frac{x(y+2) + (x-9)}{x(x-9)} = \frac{xy + 3x - 9}{x^{2} - 9x}\). Multiplying numerator and denominator by \(y\) puts it in the printed form \(\frac{xy^{2} + 3xy - 9y}{x^{2}y - 9xy}\).

whyWrong.A: The numerator is wrong and the denominator is \(xy(x-9)^{2}\) — the result of multiplying the two denominators without noticing they share the factor \((x-9)\).
whyWrong.B: This adds the numerators and adds the denominators. Fractions are never added that way.
whyWrong.D: The numerator is right but the denominator was not reduced: \(x^{3}y - 18x^{2}y + 81xy = xy(x-9)^{2}\) carries one extra factor of \((x-9)\), which cancels.

stem: If \(\frac{x}{y} = 63\) and \(\frac{cx}{3y} = 63\), what is the value of \(c\)?
whyCorrect: Rewrite the second equation as \(\frac{c}{3} \cdot \frac{x}{y} = 63\). Substituting \(\frac{x}{y} = 63\) gives \(\frac{c}{3} \cdot 63 = 63\), so \(\frac{c}{3} = 1\) and \(c = 3\). You never need the individual values of \(x\) and \(y\) — only the ratio.

stem: The function \(f\) gives the product of a number, \(x\), and a number that is 66 more than \(x\). Which equation defines \(f\)?
whyCorrect: "66 more than \(x\)" is \(x + 66\), and "product" means multiply: \(f(x) = x(x+66) = x^{2} + 66x\). Distribute the \(x\) over both terms.

whyWrong.A: This adds \(x\) and \(x+66\) rather than multiplying them, then attaches an extra \(x^{2}\).
whyWrong.B: This multiplies \(x\) by \(x\) but adds the 66 instead of multiplying it by \(x\).
whyWrong.D: The extra \(+66\) has no source; \(x(x+66)\) has only two terms.

stem: If \[8 + \frac{9(6 - x)}{4} = \frac{7(6 - x)}{3},\] what is the value of \(6 - x\)?
whyCorrect: Treat \(6-x\) as a single unknown, say \(u\), so the equation is \(8 + \frac{9u}{4} = \frac{7u}{3}\). Multiply through by 12: \(96 + 27u = 28u\), so \(u = 96\). Expanding the brackets and solving for \(x\) first works too but is far more work, and the question asks for \(6-x\), not \(x\).

stem: If \[\frac{7}{8}p + 35 = 56,\] what is the value of \(8p\)?
whyCorrect: Subtract 35: \(\frac{7}{8}p = 21\). Multiply by \(\frac{8}{7}\): \(p = 24\). The question asks for \(8p\), so the answer is \(8 \times 24 = 192\).

stem: \[(5x^{3} - 2) - (-6x^{3} + 3)\]The given expression is equivalent to \(bx^{3} - 5\), where \(b\) is a constant. What is the value of \(b\)?
whyCorrect: Distribute the minus sign over both terms of the second bracket: \(5x^{3} - 2 + 6x^{3} - 3 = 11x^{3} - 5\). Subtracting \(-6x^{3}\) adds it, which is why the coefficient is 11 and not \(-1\). Matching to \(bx^{3} - 5\) gives \(b = 11\).

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((x^{3} + 6x^{2} - 8x) + 8(x^{2} + 4)\)?
whyCorrect: Distribute the 8 first: \(8(x^{2}+4) = 8x^{2} + 32\). Then combine like terms with the first bracket: \(6x^{2} + 8x^{2} = 14x^{2}\), giving \(x^{3} + 14x^{2} - 8x + 32\).

whyWrong.A: \(4x^{2}\) is what you get by taking the 4 from inside the bracket as a coefficient; the 8 multiplies both \(x^{2}\) and 4.
whyWrong.C: This uses only the new \(8x^{2}\) and forgets to add the \(6x^{2}\) already there.
whyWrong.D: This distributes the 8 onto the constant but not onto \(x^{2}\), leaving \(6x^{2}\) unchanged.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((4x^{2} + 6) - (3x^{2})\)?
whyCorrect: Only the \(x^{2}\) terms are alike: \(4x^{2} - 3x^{2} = x^{2}\). Nothing is subtracted from the 6, so it stays \(+6\), giving \(x^{2} + 6\).

whyWrong.A: 7 comes from treating \(4x^{2}\) and 6 as combinable numbers and ignoring the variable entirely.
whyWrong.B: \(7x^{2}\) adds the coefficients when the operation is subtraction.
whyWrong.C: The sign on the 6 was flipped, but the second bracket contains only \(3x^{2}\) — there is nothing to subtract from the 6.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(\frac{y + 4}{x - 7} + \frac{y(x - 7)}{x^{2}y - 7xy}\)?
whyCorrect: Factor the second denominator: \(x^{2}y - 7xy = xy(x-7)\), so the second fraction reduces to \(\frac{y(x-7)}{xy(x-7)} = \frac{1}{x}\). Adding over the common denominator \(x(x-7)\) gives \(\frac{x(y+4) + (x-7)}{x(x-7)} = \frac{xy + 5x - 7}{x^{2}-7x}\), which is the printed choice once numerator and denominator are multiplied by \(y\).

whyWrong.A: The numerator is wrong and the denominator \(xy(x-7)^{2}\) comes from multiplying the denominators together without cancelling the shared \((x-7)\).
whyWrong.B: Numerators and denominators were added separately, which is not how fractions add.
whyWrong.D: The numerator is correct but the denominator keeps an extra factor of \((x-7)\) that cancels.

stem: If \(\frac{x}{y} = 3\) and \(\frac{5x}{ty} = 135\), what is the value of \(t\)?
whyCorrect: Split the second fraction: \(\frac{5x}{ty} = \frac{5}{t} \cdot \frac{x}{y} = \frac{5}{t} \cdot 3 = \frac{15}{t}\). Setting that equal to 135 gives \(t = \frac{15}{135} = \frac{1}{9}\). Because \(t\) is in the denominator, making the fraction much larger requires \(t\) to be small.

whyWrong.B: \(\frac{3}{5}\) comes from dividing the 3 by the 5 and ignoring the 135 entirely.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{5}{3}\) is the reciprocal of that same slip; neither uses the second equation's value.
whyWrong.D: 9 is the reciprocal of the answer — the result of solving \(15t = 135\), which would be right only if \(t\) were in the numerator.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((x^{3} + 4x^{2} - 3x) + 5(x^{2} + 8)\)?

whyWrong.B: The 5 was distributed onto the 8 but not onto \(x^{2}\), so the \(x^{2}\) term never changed.
whyWrong.C: \(8x^{2}\) uses the 8 from inside the bracket as a coefficient of \(x^{2}\); the 8 is a constant, and 5 is the multiplier.
whyWrong.D: \(5x^{2}\) is only the new term; the \(4x^{2}\) already present still has to be added in.

stem: \[\frac{2}{c} - \frac{7}{d} = 5\]The given equation relates the variables \(c\) and \(d\), where \(c\) and \(d\) are greater than 1. Which equation correctly expresses \(d\) in terms of \(c\)?
whyCorrect: Isolate the term containing \(d\): \(\frac{7}{d} = \frac{2}{c} - 5 = \frac{2 - 5c}{c}\). Now cross-multiply: \(7c = d(2-5c)\), so \(d = \frac{7c}{2-5c}\). Combining \(\frac{2}{c} - 5\) into a single fraction before flipping is the step that makes this manageable.

whyWrong.A: An extra \(c\) and 7 have been swapped; taking the reciprocal of \(\frac{2-5c}{c}\) gives \(\frac{c}{2-5c}\), which is then multiplied by 7, not divided by it.
whyWrong.C: This is the reciprocal of the correct answer — you solved for \(\frac{1}{d}\) and stopped.
whyWrong.D: Same reciprocal error with the 7 also placed in the denominator.

stem: \[ak = \frac{b}{12}(7 + m)\]The given equation relates the positive variables \(a\), \(b\), \(k\), and \(m\). Which equation correctly expresses \(m\) in terms of \(a\), \(b\), and \(k\)?
whyCorrect: Undo the multiplication before the addition. Multiply both sides by \(\frac{12}{b}\): \(\frac{12ak}{b} = 7 + m\). Then subtract 7: \(m = \frac{12ak}{b} - 7\).

whyWrong.A: Here 7 was subtracted from \(ak\) before the \(\frac{b}{12}\) was undone; the 7 is inside the bracket, so it can only be removed after dividing by \(\frac{b}{12}\).
whyWrong.B: Dividing by \(\frac{b}{12}\) is not the same as subtracting it, and the bracket was never expanded correctly.
whyWrong.C: This distributes \(\frac{b}{12}\) but then treats \(ak\) as though the \(\frac{b}{12}\) multiplying \(m\) had vanished.

stem: The product of a positive number \(x\) and the number that is 5 more than \(x\) is 104. What is the value of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: The equation is \(x(x+5) = 104\), i.e. \(x^{2} + 5x - 104 = 0\), which factors as \((x-8)(x+13)=0\). The positive solution is \(x = 8\), and indeed \(8 \times 13 = 104\).

whyWrong.C: 13 is the *other* number, \(x+5\), not \(x\) itself. It is also the discarded negative root's magnitude.
whyWrong.D: 26 is \(\frac{104}{4}\); \(26 \times 31\) is nowhere near 104.

stem: \[\frac{20}{p} = \frac{20}{q} - \frac{20}{r} - \frac{20}{s}\]The given equation relates the positive variables \(p\), \(q\), \(r\), and \(s\). Which of the following is equivalent to \(q\)?
whyCorrect: Divide everything by 20 first: \(\frac{1}{p} = \frac{1}{q} - \frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{s}\), so \(\frac{1}{q} = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{r} + \frac{1}{s}\). Put the right side over the common denominator \(prs\): \(\frac{1}{q} = \frac{rs + ps + pr}{prs}\). Taking reciprocals gives \(q = \frac{prs}{pr + rs + ps}\). The trap is that reciprocals do not add termwise.

whyWrong.A: This assumes \(\frac{1}{q} = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{r} + \frac{1}{s}\) implies \(q = p + r + s\), which is false — you cannot invert a sum term by term.
whyWrong.B: Same error, with the 20 kept even though it cancels from every term.
whyWrong.D: The 20s were carried into the denominator, but dividing the whole equation by 20 removes them; they cannot survive on one side only.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(\frac{20\pi^{2}}{\pi^{2} - x^{2}} - \frac{20\pi}{x + \pi}\)?
whyCorrect: Factor the first denominator as a difference of squares: \(\pi^{2} - x^{2} = (\pi - x)(\pi + x)\). The second fraction already has \((x+\pi)\), so multiply it by \(\frac{\pi - x}{\pi - x}\): \(\frac{20\pi(\pi - x)}{\pi^{2}-x^{2}} = \frac{20\pi^{2} - 20\pi x}{\pi^{2}-x^{2}}\). Subtracting, the \(20\pi^{2}\) terms cancel and \(\frac{20\pi x}{\pi^{2}-x^{2}}\) is left.

whyWrong.A: This cancels \(\pi\) from numerator and denominator of the first fraction before the subtraction; you cannot cancel across a sum.
whyWrong.C: This subtracts the numerators without first giving the second fraction the missing factor \((\pi - x)\).
whyWrong.D: The denominator here is not a correct factorisation of anything in the problem — \(\pi^{2}-x^{2}\) factors into \((\pi-x)(\pi+x)\).

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((6t^{4} - 3t^{2} + 3t - 6) - (2t^{4} - 4t^{3} + 6t^{2} - 6)\)?
whyCorrect: Change the sign of every term in the second bracket: \(-2t^{4} + 4t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 6\). Then combine: \(6t^{4}-2t^{4}=4t^{4}\), \(0+4t^{3}=4t^{3}\), \(-3t^{2}-6t^{2}=-9t^{2}\), \(3t\) stays, and \(-6+6=0\), so there is no constant term.

whyWrong.A: The \(3t\) changed sign even though it appears only in the first bracket, and \(-6-6=-12\) treats the second \(-6\) as if it were being added.
whyWrong.C: \(t^{3}\) instead of \(4t^{3}\) drops the coefficient, and the \(t^{2}\) and \(t\) terms have been merged.
whyWrong.D: Both the \(t^{3}\) coefficient and the \(t^{2}\) terms are wrong; \(-3t^{2}-6t^{2}\) does not vanish.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(4(x^{2} + 6)\)?
whyCorrect: The 4 multiplies everything inside the parentheses: \(4 \cdot x^{2} = 4x^{2}\) and \(4 \cdot 6 = 24\).

whyWrong.B: 10 is \(4+6\); the 4 must multiply the 6, not be added to it.
whyWrong.C: The 4 was distributed onto \(x^{2}\) only, leaving the 6 untouched.
whyWrong.D: \(-2\) is \(4-6\), subtracting instead of multiplying.

stem: \[b - 22 = \frac{x}{y}\]The given equation relates positive numbers \(b\), \(x\), and \(y\). Which equation correctly expresses \(x\) in terms of \(b\) and \(y\)?
whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \(y\). The \(y\) must multiply the whole left side, not just part of it: \(x = y(b-22) = by - 22y\).

whyWrong.A: Dividing by \(y\) is the wrong direction — \(x\) is already divided by \(y\) in the original, so undoing that multiplies.
whyWrong.B: Here \(y\) was multiplied onto \(b\) only. Distribute it over both terms of \(b-22\).
whyWrong.D: This divides by \(y\) instead of multiplying, which would be right if the original read \(b - 22 = xy\).

stem: The expression \(72y^{5} - 48y^{4}\) is equivalent to \(ry^{4}(12y - 8)\), where \(r\) is a constant. What is the value of \(r\)?
whyCorrect: Expand the target form: \(ry^{4}(12y-8) = 12ry^{5} - 8ry^{4}\). Matching the \(y^{5}\) terms gives \(12r = 72\), so \(r = 6\); the \(y^{4}\) terms confirm it, since \(8 \times 6 = 48\).

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(11(x^{2} - 100y^{2})\)?
whyCorrect: \(x^{2} - 100y^{2}\) is a difference of squares, since \(100y^{2} = (10y)^{2}\). So it factors as \((x-10y)(x+10y)\), and the 11 stays outside.

whyWrong.A: Multiplying out gives \(x^{2} - 52xy + 100y^{2}\) — both the middle term and the sign of the last term are wrong.
whyWrong.B: This expands to \(x^{2} + 48xy - 100y^{2}\); the \(xy\) term must cancel, which only happens when the two numbers are equal and opposite.
whyWrong.C: This is \((x-10y)^{2} = x^{2} - 20xy + 100y^{2}\), a perfect square, not a difference of squares.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((9c + 8) - (4c^{3} - 6)\)?
whyCorrect: Distribute the minus over both terms: \(9c + 8 - 4c^{3} + 6\). Subtracting \(-6\) adds 6, so the constant is \(8 + 6 = 14\), and the cubic term becomes \(-4c^{3}\).

whyWrong.A: Both signs are wrong: the \(4c^{3}\) should become negative and the \(-6\) should become \(+6\).
whyWrong.B: The constant 14 is right but the \(4c^{3}\) kept its sign; it is being subtracted.
whyWrong.C: The cubic sign is right, but \(8 - 6 = 2\) treats the \(-6\) as if it were still being subtracted.

stem: The kinetic energy \(K\), in joules, of an object is given by the formula \(K = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\), where \(m\) is the mass of the object, in kilograms, and \(v\) is the velocity of the object, in meters per second. If the kinetic energy of a certain object can be found by using the formula \(K = 32v^{2}\), what is the mass of the object, in kilograms?
whyCorrect: Compare the two formulas term by term. The coefficient of \(v^{2}\) is \(\frac{1}{2}m\) in one and 32 in the other, so \(\frac{1}{2}m = 32\) and \(m = 64\).

whyWrong.A: 1,024 is \(32^{2}\); the 32 is not squared, only \(v\) is.
whyWrong.C: 32 is the coefficient itself, which equals \(\frac{1}{2}m\), not \(m\).
whyWrong.D: 16 is \(\frac{32}{2}\); you divided by 2 where you should have multiplied, since \(m\) is being halved in the formula.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(11x^{3} + 2x^{2} + 7x\)?
whyCorrect: Every term contains at least one \(x\) and the coefficients 11, 2 and 7 share no common factor, so the only thing to factor out is \(x\): \(x(11x^{2} + 2x + 7)\). Check by distributing back.

whyWrong.A: Expanding gives \(20x^{3} + 20x^{2} + 20x\); the coefficients 11, 2 and 7 are different from each other, so no single number factors out.
whyWrong.C: Expanding gives \(77x^{4} + 14x^{3} + 7x\) — the degree is wrong, because \(7x\) was pulled out while the terms inside kept their original powers.
whyWrong.D: Identical to choice A and wrong for the same reason.

note: Choices A and D are printed identically (both 20(x^3+x^2+x)); the question effectively has only three distinct options.

stem: \[\frac{49}{p} = \frac{49}{q} - \frac{49}{r} - \frac{49}{s}\]The given equation relates the positive variables \(p\), \(q\), \(r\), and \(s\). Which of the following is equivalent to \(q\)?
whyCorrect: Divide the whole equation by 49: \(\frac{1}{p} = \frac{1}{q} - \frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{s}\), so \(\frac{1}{q} = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{r} + \frac{1}{s} = \frac{rs + ps + pr}{prs}\). Inverting both sides gives \(q = \frac{prs}{pr + ps + rs}\). Reciprocals cannot be added term by term, which is what makes this more than one step.

whyWrong.A: This inverts a sum of reciprocals term by term, which is not valid: \(\frac{1}{q}=\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{r}+\frac{1}{s}\) does not give \(q=p+r+s\).
whyWrong.B: The same invalid inversion, with a stray 49 that actually cancels out of every term.
whyWrong.D: The 49 divides out of the whole equation, so it cannot remain in the denominator of the answer.

stem: If \(\frac{j}{k} = 62\) and \(\frac{96j}{12xk} = 62\), what is the value of \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Separate the constants from the ratio: \(\frac{96j}{12xk} = \frac{96}{12x} \cdot \frac{j}{k} = \frac{8}{x} \cdot 62\). Setting that equal to 62 gives \(\frac{8}{x} = 1\), so \(x = 8\). You never need \(j\) or \(k\) individually.

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{1}{8}\) is the reciprocal — it solves \(8x = 1\) instead of \(\frac{8}{x} = 1\).
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{6}{31}\) comes from dividing 12 by 62 and simplifying; the 62s cancel and never enter the answer.
whyWrong.D: 96 uses only the numerator's constant and ignores the 12 in the denominator.

stem: If \(\frac{42}{x} = 7x\), what is the value of \(7x^{2}\)?
whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \(x\): \(42 = 7x^{2}\). That is exactly what the question asks for, so the answer is 42 — there is no need to find \(x\) itself.

whyWrong.A: 6 is the value of \(x^{2}\), one factor of 7 short of what was asked.
whyWrong.B: 7 is just the coefficient in the expression, not its value.
whyWrong.D: 294 is \(42 \times 7\); the 7 is already included once you multiply \(\frac{42}{x}=7x\) by \(x\).

stem: \[b - 72 = \frac{x}{y}\]The given equation relates the positive numbers \(b\), \(x\), and \(y\). Which equation correctly expresses \(x\) in terms of \(b\) and \(y\)?
whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \(y\), and let it multiply the entire left side: \(x = y(b - 72) = by - 72y\).

whyWrong.A: Dividing by \(y\) is the wrong operation; \(x\) is already divided by \(y\), so undoing it multiplies.
whyWrong.B: The \(y\) was distributed onto \(b\) only. The 72 is inside the same expression and must be multiplied too.
whyWrong.C: This multiplies by \(y\) and then divides by \(y\) again, which undoes the step.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((3nr^{2} + 4nr) + (8n^{2}r + 2nr)\)?
whyCorrect: Only \(4nr\) and \(2nr\) are like terms, giving \(6nr\). \(3nr^{2}\) and \(8n^{2}r\) have different variable parts, so neither combines with anything and both are carried through unchanged.

whyWrong.A: This adds \(3nr^{2}\) and \(8n^{2}r\) as if they were like terms; \(nr^{2}\) and \(n^{2}r\) are not the same.
whyWrong.B: Same false combination plus invented exponents; adding terms never changes the powers.
whyWrong.C: 24 is \(3 \times 8\) and 8 is \(4 \times 2\) — the terms were multiplied instead of added.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(63x^{2}\)?
whyCorrect: \((7x)(9x) = 63x^{2}\): multiply the coefficients \(7 \times 9 = 63\) and add the exponents, \(x^{1} \cdot x^{1} = x^{2}\).

whyWrong.A: This expands to \(63 + 63x^{2}\), which has an extra constant term.
whyWrong.C: Adding the exponents here gives \(63x^{4}\), not \(63x^{2}\).
whyWrong.D: This is \(63x^{3}\) — one power of \(x\) too many.

stem: \[v = -\frac{w}{188x}\]The given equation relates the distinct positive numbers \(v\), \(w\), and \(x\). Which equation correctly expresses \(w\) in terms of \(v\) and \(x\)?
whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \(188x\): \(188xv = -w\), so \(w = -188vx\). The \(x\) sits in the denominator on the right, so undoing that division makes it a factor.

whyWrong.B: This keeps \(x\) in the denominator; \(w\) was divided by \(x\), so recovering \(w\) multiplies by \(x\).
whyWrong.C: This inverts the relationship, putting \(v\) in the denominator when \(v\) is alone on the left and becomes a factor.
whyWrong.D: The relationship is multiplicative, so terms cannot be moved across the equals sign by adding.

stem: \[49 = \frac{2K}{v^{2}}\]For an object with a mass of 49 kilograms, the given equation relates the kinetic energy \(K\), in joules, of the object to the object's speed \(v\), in meters per second, where \(K\) and \(v\) are positive. Which equation correctly expresses this object's speed, in meters per second, in terms of the object's kinetic energy, in joules?
whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \(v^{2}\): \(49v^{2} = 2K\). Divide by 49: \(v^{2} = \frac{2K}{49}\). Then take the positive square root, since \(v > 0\): \(v = \sqrt{\frac{2K}{49}}\).

whyWrong.B: This is the reciprocal inside the root — it comes from dividing in the wrong direction when clearing \(v^{2}\).
whyWrong.C: Squaring the 49 instead of taking a square root of the whole expression; the square is on \(v\), not on 49.
whyWrong.D: Same error, and no square root is taken at all, so the units and the algebra both fail.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(158t^{3} - 24t^{2}u\)?
whyCorrect: The common factor is \(2t^{2}\): both coefficients are even (158 = 2·79, 24 = 2·12) and both terms have at least \(t^{2}\). Only the second term has \(u\), so \(u\) cannot come out. That leaves \(2t^{2}(79t - 12u)\).

whyWrong.A: Expanding gives \(158t^{3} - 24tu\); one factor of \(t\) is missing from the second term.
whyWrong.C: \(u\) cannot be factored out because the first term \(158t^{3}\) contains no \(u\); expanding gives \(158t^{3}u\).
whyWrong.D: Same problem — pulling \(u\) out puts a \(u\) into the first term that was never there.

stem: The expression \(19x^{5} + 20x^{5} - 10x^{5}\) is equivalent to \(bx^{5}\), where \(b\) is a constant. What is the value of \(b\)?
whyCorrect: All three terms have the same variable part \(x^{5}\), so just combine the coefficients: \(19 + 20 - 10 = 29\). The power stays \(x^{5}\), so \(b = 29\).

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((133y)^{\frac{1}{2}}\), where \(y > 1\)?
whyCorrect: An exponent of \(\frac{1}{2}\) is a square root, and it applies to everything inside the parentheses, so \((133y)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{133y}\).

whyWrong.A: Only \(y\) was put under the root; the 133 is inside the parentheses too.
whyWrong.B: Only the 133 was put under the root, leaving \(y\) outside.
whyWrong.D: Squaring and then rooting returns \(133y\) itself for positive values — that is the original quantity, not its square root.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(4yz^{3} + 5yz + 3yz^{3}\)?
whyCorrect: \(4yz^{3}\) and \(3yz^{3}\) are like terms, so add their coefficients to get \(7yz^{3}\). \(5yz\) has a different power of \(z\), so it cannot be combined with them.

whyWrong.B: Adding like terms does not add the exponents; \(z^{3}+z^{3}\) is \(2z^{3}\), not \(z^{6}\).
whyWrong.C: 12 comes from multiplying \(4 \times 3\), and \(5yz\) has been absorbed even though it is not a like term.
whyWrong.D: Same two errors, with the exponents of all three terms added together.

stem: If \(\frac{x}{y} = 76\) and \(\frac{cx}{4y} = 76\), what is the value of \(c\)?
whyCorrect: Write the second equation as \(\frac{c}{4} \cdot \frac{x}{y} = 76\). Substituting \(\frac{x}{y} = 76\) gives \(\frac{c}{4} \cdot 76 = 76\), so \(\frac{c}{4} = 1\) and \(c = 4\). Both expressions equal the same number, so the extra factor \(\frac{c}{4}\) must be 1.

stem: If \(\frac{72}{x} = 6x\), what is the value of \(6x^{2}\)?
whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \(x\): \(72 = 6x^{2}\). The expression asked for is already on the right, so the answer is 72 — solving for \(x\) is unnecessary.

whyWrong.A: 432 is \(72 \times 6\); the factor of 6 is already included once you clear the denominator.
whyWrong.C: 12 is \(x^{2}\) (since \(x^{2}=12\)), missing the coefficient 6.
whyWrong.D: 6 is only the coefficient in the expression, not its value.

stem: The expression \(7x^{6} + 9x^{6} - 8x^{6}\) is equivalent to \(bx^{6}\), where \(b\) is a constant. What is the value of \(b\)?
whyCorrect: All three terms share the variable part \(x^{6}\), so combine the coefficients: \(7 + 9 - 8 = 8\). The exponent is unchanged, so \(b = 8\).

stem: \[\frac{46}{p} = \frac{46}{q} - \frac{46}{r} - \frac{46}{s}\]The given equation relates the positive variables \(p\), \(q\), \(r\), and \(s\). Which of the following is equivalent to \(q\)?
whyCorrect: Divide through by 46: \(\frac{1}{p} = \frac{1}{q} - \frac{1}{r} - \frac{1}{s}\), so \(\frac{1}{q} = \frac{1}{p} + \frac{1}{r} + \frac{1}{s}\). Over the common denominator \(prs\) that is \(\frac{rs + ps + pr}{prs}\), and taking reciprocals gives \(q = \frac{prs}{pr + ps + rs}\).

whyWrong.B: The 46 cancels from every term when you divide the equation by it; it cannot survive in the denominator.
whyWrong.C: Reciprocals do not add term by term — \(\frac{1}{q}=\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{r}+\frac{1}{s}\) does not mean \(q=p+r+s\).
whyWrong.D: Same invalid inversion, with the 46 kept even though it cancels.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(30x^{2} + 6x + 6\)?
whyCorrect: All three coefficients are divisible by 6: \(30 = 6 \cdot 5\), \(6 = 6 \cdot 1\), \(6 = 6 \cdot 1\). Factoring gives \(6(5x^{2} + x + 1)\); distribute back to check.

whyWrong.A: This divides only the first coefficient by 6 and leaves the others alone, so it is not equal to the original.
whyWrong.B: Expanding gives \(30x^{2} + 30x\), which loses the constant term and changes the middle coefficient.
whyWrong.D: 42 is \(30 + 6 + 6\); the three terms are not like terms and cannot be added together.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(3xy(2x^{2} + 7y)\)?
whyCorrect: Distribute \(3xy\) over both terms, multiplying coefficients and adding exponents: \(3xy \cdot 2x^{2} = 6x^{3}y\) and \(3xy \cdot 7y = 21xy^{2}\).

whyWrong.A: The coefficients were added instead of multiplied (\(3+2=5\), \(3+7=10\)).
whyWrong.B: The \(3xy\) was applied only partially — the \(x\) never reached the first term's exponent and the second term never got multiplied at all.
whyWrong.C: The exponents were not increased: \(x \cdot x^{2} = x^{3}\) and \(y \cdot y = y^{2}\).

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(20x^{2} + 3 + 5x^{2}\)?
whyCorrect: \(20x^{2}\) and \(5x^{2}\) are like terms, so their coefficients add to give \(25x^{2}\). The constant 3 has no like term and stays as it is.

whyWrong.A: Adding like terms leaves the exponent alone; \(x^{2}+x^{2}\) is not \(x^{4}\).
whyWrong.C: 28 comes from adding the 3 into the coefficient, but 3 is a constant, not an \(x^{2}\) term.
whyWrong.D: Same error — the constant cannot be absorbed into the \(x^{2}\) coefficient.

stem: A right rectangular prism has a base area of \(56t\) square centimeters (cm²). The length of the base of the rectangular prism is \(\frac{14}{3}\) cm, and the height of the rectangular prism is 3 cm. Which expression represents the surface area, in cm², of the right rectangular prism?
whyCorrect: First get the base width: area ÷ length \(= 56t \div \frac{14}{3} = 56t \cdot \frac{3}{14} = 12t\). Surface area is two bases plus the side faces: \(2(56t) + (\text{base perimeter})(\text{height}) = 112t + 2\left(\frac{14}{3} + 12t\right)(3) = 112t + 28 + 72t = 184t + 28\).

whyWrong.A: This doubles the base area and then adds 56 instead of computing the four side faces from the perimeter.
whyWrong.C: 1,680 comes from multiplying rather than dividing when finding the width, inflating the side-face contribution.
whyWrong.D: This omits the constant term entirely, which comes from the two faces whose area is \(\frac{14}{3} \times 3\) each.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(7x^{5} - 6x^{4} + 9x^{3}\)?
whyCorrect: The lowest power present is \(x^{3}\), and 7, 6 and 9 share no common factor, so factor out \(x^{3}\) only: \(x^{3}(7x^{2} - 6x + 9)\).

whyWrong.A: Expanding gives \(7x^{5} - 6x^{4}\); the \(9x^{3}\) term has disappeared.
whyWrong.C: 9 is not a factor of 7 or 6, and expanding gives \(63x^{5} - 54x^{4} + 9x^{3}\).
whyWrong.D: Expanding gives terms of degree 9 and 8; you cannot factor out a power higher than the lowest one present.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(5xy + 30x^{2}y + 35xy^{2}\)?
whyCorrect: Every term contains \(5xy\). Dividing each term by \(5xy\) gives \(1\), \(6x\) and \(7y\), so the factored form is \(5xy(1 + 6x + 7y)\). The first term leaves a 1 behind, not nothing.

whyWrong.A: The coefficients inside were not divided by 5; expanding gives \(5xy + 150x^{2}y + 175xy^{2}\).
whyWrong.C: The \(5xy\) term vanished. Factoring a term out of itself leaves 1, which must stay inside the bracket.
whyWrong.D: Same missing 1 — expanding gives only two terms, not three.

stem: The kinetic energy \(K\), in joules, of an object is given by the formula \(K = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}\), where \(m\) is the mass of the object, in kilograms, and \(v\) is the velocity of the object, in meters per second. If the kinetic energy of a certain object can be found by using the formula \(K = 98v^{2}\), what is the mass of the object, in kilograms?
whyCorrect: Match the coefficients of \(v^{2}\) in the two formulas: \(\frac{1}{2}m = 98\), so \(m = 196\).

whyWrong.A: 9,604 is \(98^{2}\); only \(v\) is squared in the formula, not the coefficient.
whyWrong.C: 98 is \(\frac{1}{2}m\), not \(m\) — one doubling short.
whyWrong.D: 49 halves the coefficient again; since the formula already halves \(m\), recovering \(m\) means doubling.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \((5x^{3} - 3x + 8) - (9x^{6} + 5x - 3)\)?
whyCorrect: Distribute the minus sign: \(5x^{3} - 3x + 8 - 9x^{6} - 5x + 3\). Now combine: \(-9x^{6}\) stands alone, \(5x^{3}\) stands alone, \(-3x - 5x = -8x\), and \(8 + 3 = 11\).

whyWrong.A: \(-4x^{9}\) comes from subtracting \(9x^{6}\) from \(5x^{3}\) as though they were like terms; different powers never combine.
whyWrong.C: The signs on the second bracket's last two terms were not changed: \(-3x - 5x\) is \(-8x\), and \(8-(-3)\) is 11.
whyWrong.D: Both errors — the unlike powers were merged and the constants were subtracted instead of added.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(2x^{3} + 8x^{2}y + xy^{2} + 4y^{3}\)?
whyCorrect: Factor by grouping. The first pair gives \(2x^{2}(x + 4y)\) and the second pair gives \(y^{2}(x + 4y)\). Both share \((x+4y)\), so the expression is \((2x^{2} + y^{2})(x + 4y)\). If your grouping does not leave the same bracket twice, regroup.

whyWrong.A: Expanding gives \(2x^{3} + 2x^{2}y^{2} + 4xy + 4y^{3}\) — the two middle terms are wrong.
whyWrong.C: The degrees are too high; expanding produces \(x^{5}\) terms, which the original does not have.
whyWrong.D: Expanding gives \(2x^{4} + 8x^{3}y + xy^{3} + 4y^{4}\), one degree too high throughout.

stem: \[b - 49 = \frac{x}{y}\]The given equation relates the positive numbers \(b\), \(x\), and \(y\). Which equation correctly expresses \(x\) in terms of \(b\) and \(y\)?
whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \(y\), letting it act on the whole left side: \(x = y(b - 49) = by - 49y\).

whyWrong.A: Multiplying and then dividing by \(y\) undoes the step; this is not equal to \(y(b-49)\).
whyWrong.C: Only \(b\) was multiplied by \(y\). The 49 is part of the same expression and must be multiplied as well.
whyWrong.D: Dividing by \(y\) goes the wrong way — \(x\) is already divided by \(y\) in the original equation.

stem: If \(\frac{2a}{b} = 6.5\) and \(\frac{a}{bn} = 26\), what is the value of \(n\)?
whyCorrect: Halve the first equation to get \(\frac{a}{b} = 3.25\). The second is \(\frac{a}{b} \cdot \frac{1}{n} = 26\), so \(\frac{3.25}{n} = 26\) and \(n = \frac{3.25}{26} = 0.125 = \frac{1}{8}\). Watch the two traps: halve 6.5 first, and the question asks for \(n\), not \(\frac{1}{n}\) (which is 8).
note: Free-response answer is 1/8; the equivalent decimal .125 should also be accepted.

stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(14(x^{2} - 6)\)?
whyCorrect: The 14 multiplies both terms inside: \(14 \cdot x^{2} = 14x^{2}\) and \(14 \cdot (-6) = -84\).

whyWrong.B: \(-20\) is \(-14-6\); the 14 must multiply the 6, not be added to it.
whyWrong.C: The 14 was distributed onto \(x^{2}\) only, leaving the \(-6\) untouched.
whyWrong.D: \(+8\) is \(14-6\), which both subtracts instead of multiplying and flips the sign.

stem: \[0.24x^{2} + 0.56x + 1.52\]The given expression can be rewritten as \(a(3x^{2} + 7x + 19)\), where \(a\) is a constant. What is the value of \(a\)?
whyCorrect: Each coefficient of the original must be \(a\) times the matching coefficient inside the bracket: \(0.24 = 3a\) gives \(a = 0.08\). Check the others: \(7 \times 0.08 = 0.56\) and \(19 \times 0.08 = 1.52\), so all three agree.

stem: If (x + 9) − 5 = 25, what is the value of x + 9?
whyCorrect: Treat \(x+9\) as a single block: adding 5 to both sides gives \(x + 9 = 30\) immediately. There is no need to find \(x\) (which is 21).

whyWrong.B: 21 is the value of \(x\), not \(x+9\). The question asks for the whole expression.
whyWrong.C: 20 is \(25-5\); the 5 is being subtracted on the left, so undoing it means adding 5 to 25.
whyWrong.D: 11 comes from subtracting 9 as well and mixing up which quantity is being asked for.

stem: If 5(x + 1) = 25, what is the value of x + 1?
whyCorrect: Divide both sides by 5, keeping \(x+1\) intact: \(x + 1 = 5\). (\(x\) itself is 4, but that is not what was asked.)

whyWrong.A: 4 is the value of \(x\); the question asks for \(x+1\).
whyWrong.C: 19 is \(25-5-1\); the 5 multiplies the bracket, so it is removed by division, not subtraction.
whyWrong.D: 20 is \(25-5\), subtracting the coefficient instead of dividing by it.

stem: What value of x is the solution to the equation x + 10 = 3?
whyCorrect: Subtract 10 from both sides: \(x = 3 - 10 = -7\). Since 10 is being added to \(x\) and the result is smaller than 10, \(x\) must be negative.

whyWrong.A: \(-13\) is \(-3-10\); the 3 is positive on the right side.
whyWrong.C: 7 is \(10-3\), the subtraction done in the wrong order.
whyWrong.D: 13 is \(3+10\); adding 10 undoes nothing here — the 10 is already on the left with \(x\).

stem:
\(|3x - 12| = 18\)

What is the sum of the solutions to the given equation?
